frontiers.matches: Compiler version confirmed by direct self-identification: compiling tests/fixtures/probe1.c with the pinned TCC.EXE produces an OMF THEADR/COMENT record containing the literal string 'TC86 Borland Turbo C++ 1.00', matching the 'Turbo C++ - Copyright 1990 Borland Intl.' runtime string already found embedded in build/DAVE_unpacked.exe. See docs/toolchain-identification.md. Toolchain (TCC.EXE/TLINK.EXE/TLIB.EXE + per-model libraries) obtained from archive.org's Vintage Software Collection and pinned by SHA-256 in layout/toolchain.json; DOSBox-X (C:/DOSBox-X/dosbox-x.exe) drives compilation via tools/compile_probe.py. Regression-tested in tests/test_toolchain_probe.py.
frontiers.first_unresolved_fact: Compiler identity is settled. Not yet determined: Dangerous Dave's actual memory model and optimization flags (compact model / -1- -f- -N- used only as an untested starting guess), and whether TASM (not present in this disk set) is needed for any hand-written ASM.
frontiers.unblock: N/A for compiler identity — closed. Next: function census on RAW_LOAD_MODULE to find real isolated functions to compare codegen against, to pin down memory model/flags.
frontiers.leverage: Toolchain is now installed, pinned, and proven end-to-end (compile -> OMF parse) — unblocks all future matching-C probe work without further acquisition steps.

frontiers.target: Initial function census over RAW_LOAD_MODULE (starting with _main)
frontiers.matches: STARTUP_C0S's self-relative CALL fixup to external '_main' (offset 253 in C0S.OBJ's _TEXT, file offset 765) resolves to load-module offset 0x439 = file offset 0x639 -- this is the linker-computed, unambiguous address of the game's main() function.
frontiers.first_unresolved_fact: Linear disassembly starting exactly at file offset 0x639 does not show the standard 'push bp; mov bp,sp' prologue that this exact pinned compiler (TCC 1.00, small model, flags -1- -f- -N-) reliably emits for any function using bp-relative locals (confirmed empirically: tests/fixtures/probe2.c compiles to '55 8b ec 83 ec 1a ...' under identical flags). The bytes immediately preceding 0x639 ('...52 e8 de9f 83 c4 06') look like they could alternatively be read as ending with 'add sp,6' bleeding 2 bytes into what I assumed was 0x639's start, i.e. a possible off-by-N instruction-boundary misalignment somewhere in this region. Not yet resolved.
frontiers.unblock: Systematic function-boundary analysis: sweep backward/forward from known anchors (the STARTUP_C0S->'_main' call, and other C0S external call targets like '_exit') using RET/RETF opcode boundaries and call-target cross-references rather than naive linear disassembly from one computed address; verify against several more compiled probes matching the addressing idioms observed (e.g. imul by small odd constants suggesting sizeof(struct)==9 or 7 array indexing).
frontiers.leverage: This is the entry point for the entire function census (Phase 2) and the first real matching-C candidate; resolving it unlocks systematic disassembly of the whole 171,767-byte RAW_LOAD_MODULE region.

frontiers.target: Obtain TASM (Turbo Assembler) for MATCHING_ASM promotion
frontiers.matches: None — the acquired Turbo C++ 1.0 disk set only included TASM2MSG.EXE (a message-file converter), not TASM.EXE itself.
frontiers.first_unresolved_fact: TASM was historically sold both bundled with certain Turbo C++ SKUs and as a standalone product; the exact TASM version paired with this specific Turbo C++ 1.0 release is unknown.
frontiers.unblock: Locate a legitimately obtainable TASM 1.x/2.x installation (e.g. archive.org) once a candidate hand-written-ASM region is identified during function census, and confirm its version the same way TCC was confirmed (self-identifying strings in generated .OBJ if any, or matching known TASM release timelines to 1990).
frontiers.leverage: Only needed once MATCHING_ASM promotion begins; MATCHING_C work is unblocked without it.

end_state: Independent source modules (matching C, matching ASM, structured data/assets) compile, assemble, and link with a historically faithful toolchain such that the resulting unpacked executable image is byte-identical to the original, addresses emerge from module composition rather than being copied, and the image can subsequently be re-packed with LZEXE 0.91 to reproduce the original DAVE.EXE exactly. EGADAVE.DAV resources are simultaneously reconstructed from human-readable canonical sources (images, tables) plus deterministic encoders.
